articles.title: Cloudflare separates AI training opt-outs from search crawling for publishers
articles.description: New Delhi: Cloudflare has introduced a new control that allows website owners to opt out of AI training without necessarily shutting out the same companies from crawling their sites for traditional search. The “Disallow AI Training” setting is aimed at what Cloudflare calls “mixed-use crawlers”, which can be used both to build search indexes and to collect content for AI training. Until now, publishers dealing with such crawlers could face a trade-off: blocking a crawler to prevent AI training could also affect the crawler’s ability to index the site for search. Under the new system, website owners can signal that their content should not be used for AI training while continuing to allow eligible crawlers to access the site for search indexing. The control, however, depends on crawler operators respecting those signals, and implementation is not uniform across all platforms. Cloudflare has also acknowledged that some controls, including Microsoft’s broader site-wide training opt-out, are still being developed. Cloudflare said Apple, Google and Microsoft meet or have committed to meeting the requirements it has set for what it calls “Accountable” crawler operators. To qualify, operators must provide or commit to providing a way for websites to opt out of AI training, a mechanism to express preferences around AI summaries, URL-level visibility into which pages were available for training, and an assurance that refusing AI training will not affect traditional search results. Cloudflare said fewer than 1% of sites on its network block search bots, while 17% have enabled some mechanism to block AI training. The gap points to a distinction publishers are increasingly making between search indexing and the use of their content for training AI models. Search, training and AI agents separated Cloudflare is reorganising its controls around three categories: Search, Training and Agent. Search covers crawling used to build a search index. Training refers to crawling for training or fine-tuning AI models. Agent traffic covers AI systems that access webpages on behalf of users, including chat-fetch bots and browser-use agents. Website owners will be able to choose between allowing crawlers, disallowing AI training, blocking crawlers only on pages carrying advertising, or blocking them entirely. Under the Disallow AI Training setting, Cloudflare said eligible mixed-use crawlers can continue accessing content for search while being instructed not to use that content for training. Training-only crawlers operated by companies including Amazon, Anthropic, Meta and OpenAI can be blocked separately without affecting search because those companies use different crawlers for search and training purposes, according to Cloudflare. Cloudflare is also phasing out its broader “Block AI Bots” control in favour of separate settings for Search, Training and Agent traffic. If a publisher chooses to block mixed-use crawlers completely, the setting will also block Applebot, Bingbot and Googlebot, which would prevent those services from crawling the site for search as well. Different default for ad-supported publishers Cloudflare is also recommending a different configuration for newly onboarded websites that say they make money from advertising. From September 15, such domains will be offered a setting that allows search, disallows AI training and blocks AI agents on pages serving ads. Cloudflare said ad-supported publishers face a different trade-off because their revenue often depends on users reaching the original webpage. AI systems may consume or retrieve content without generating the same visit. New domains that do not rely on advertising will be offered a less restrictive default that allows search, training and agent access, although website owners can change those settings. Google, Apple and Microsoft take different approaches Google already allows website owners to opt out of certain AI uses without affecting their visibility in search. Cloudflare said Google is also developing tools intended to give publishers more clarity on how individual webpages may be used. Apple similarly allows publishers to keep their content out of AI training and express preferences around how it appears in AI-generated summaries. According to Cloudflare, opting out of training does not affect a site’s search ranking. Microsoft also gives website owners some control over whether their content can be used for AI training. It is working on a broader site-wide opt-out, which Cloudflare said is expected in early 2027. Until that is available, Cloudflare’s new setting will not automatically communicate a publisher’s no-training preference to Bing. AI summaries are the next issue Separating search crawling from AI training does not resolve another issue facing publishers: how much of their content can appear inside AI-generated answers and summaries. Cloudflare said a simple allow-or-block choice may not be enough because publishers may also want control over how much of an article or webpage can be reproduced in an AI-generated response. The company plans to work towards controls that would let website owners set preferences around the amount of their content that can appear in AI summaries. Its stated goal is to provide a centralised control through Cloudflare by early next year rather than require publishers to manage preferences separately across different platforms. The change comes as publishers, AI companies and internet infrastructure providers continue to work out separate rules for search indexing, model training and AI-generated answers. Standards and controls remain uneven across platforms, and publishers still have to rely on individual crawler operators to honour the preferences they set.

articles.title: India’s creative jobs account for 19% of work AI use, 60% higher than global average: Google
articles.description: New Delhi: Creative occupations account for 19% of work-related AI usage in India, a share that is 1.6 times, or about 60% higher than the global average, according to new data released by Google. The finding comes from Google’s AI & Economy ATLAS, which tracks how people across countries and occupations are using artificial intelligence. Google said the 19% share comes from occupations spanning arts, design and media, making these creative roles one of the more prominent areas of work-related AI usage in India. The number does not mean that 19% of Indian creative professionals use AI. Rather, creative occupations account for 19% of the work-related AI activity captured in Google’s dataset in India. The pattern is markedly different from the US, where AI usage is much more concentrated in technical jobs. Computer and mathematical occupations account for 30% of work-related AI usage in the US, twice their share in the rest of the world. Google’s data suggests that there is no single occupational pattern for AI adoption across markets. The kinds of jobs turning to AI most frequently vary depending on the country and broader economic context. One of the clearest differences emerges when Google compares OECD and non-OECD economies. The OECD, or Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, is a 38-member grouping that includes countries such as the US, UK, Germany, France, Japan, South Korea, Australia and Canada. India is not an OECD member, although it has been one of the organisation’s five Key Partners since 2007, alongside Brazil, China, Indonesia and South Africa. In OECD countries, computer and mathematical occupations and business and financial operations lead AI usage. The picture changes outside the OECD. In non-OECD economies, the leading groups include office and administrative support; arts, design, entertainment, sports and media; and educational instruction and library occupations. India falls within this non-OECD grouping in Google’s analysis. The OECD distinction should not, however, be read simply as a divide between developed and developing economies. It is an institutional grouping, and some of the world’s largest economies, including India and China, are not members. Google also found that AI adoption generally increases with a country’s income level, but the relationship is not uniform. Brazil and the UAE show higher levels of AI adoption than their GDP per capita would predict, according to the ATLAS data. Differences also emerge in the kinds of work for which AI is being used. In Brazil and Germany, 7% of work-related AI usage goes towards manual tasks, including applications such as real-time equipment diagnostics and troubleshooting. That is 1.4 times the global average. In Japan, manual tasks account for 4% of work-related AI use. Google has now opened up more of the ATLAS data through an interactive public tool. Users can compare AI adoption across occupations, examine how AI is being used outside the workplace and look at adoption rates across countries. Google said the occupational data ranges from professions such as electricians to purchasing managers. The latest ATLAS update also looks separately at how scientists are using AI. Research from Google and Google DeepMind, in collaboration with MIT FutureTech, analysed 2,600 specialised AI models and surveyed more than 600 scientists in the US and UK. Nearly half of the scientists surveyed said they use some form of AI every day. The research found that both large language models and specialised AI models are being used in science, but often for different purposes. LLM use is spread across scientific fields and tasks, while specialised models are relatively more common in health and life sciences and for areas such as domain-specific prediction, generation and simulation. Scientists reported saving almost seven hours a week through the use of AI. But Google said faster work at one stage of research is also creating bottlenecks elsewhere, including a backlog of hypotheses awaiting further testing. For India, however, one of the more distinctive findings in the latest data remains the weight of creative work in AI usage. While technical occupations dominate the US picture, creative occupations are taking a disproportionately larger share of work-related AI activity in India.

articles.title: R400k reward offered in Ekurhuleni women's deaths probe
articles.description: R400k reward offered in Ekurhuleni women's deaths probe Zandile.Khumalo Wed, 09/16/2026 - 06:10 SAPS vehicles at a crime scene JOHANNESBURG - An amount of R400,000 has been put on the table for anyone with information that could assist in the investigation into the deaths of eight women whose bodies were discovered in Ekurhuleni. This is one of several measures being implemented as investigations into the matter continue. Other measures include the establishment of a high-level multidisciplinary team to lead the investigation. There will also be an increased police presence through Operation Shanela in Kempton Park and surrounding areas. READ | Police keep cards close to chest amid probe in Ekurhuleni murders This was confirmed during a media briefing on Tuesday night following a meeting between senior police and government officials. The high-level delegation included Acting Police Minister Firoz Cachalia, Women Minister Sindisiwe Chikunga, Deputy Police Minister Polly Boshielo, Gauteng Premier Panyaza Lesufi and Acting National Police Commissioner Puleng Dimpane. Cachalia said police would “lock down” Kempton Park in the coming weeks. “The community will see the presence of the South African Police Service, and we will mobilise all necessary law enforcement capabilities, working with our communities,” he said. Also read: Discovery of eighth body added to investigations into Ekurhuleni murders
